title: How Foreign Accent Syndrome Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a TryPod March promotion and a British-accent bit, then discuss code switching (adopting another group's accent) and how it differs from foreign accent syndrome (FAS), a rare condition in which brain damage or psychological causes change a person's speech prosody so it sounds like a foreign accent. They cover case examples: Lisa Arlami (Texas woman with a British-sounding accent after jaw surgery), Astrid of Norway (German-sounding accent after WWII shrapnel brain injury, coined by neurologist Herman Monrad-Krohn's term prosodyas), Harry Whittaker's coined term and four-point diagnostic criteria, neurogenic vs psychogenic vs mixed FAS, a US schizophrenia case with a British accent, Sarah Colwill of England with a Chinese-sounding accent after migraines, and a Dutch teacher who spoke Dutch with French features. They debate whether the accent is only in the ear of the listener and how brain damage affects prosody. The episode ends with listener mail and thank-yous for gifts and letters.

segments.title: Opening banter and TryPod month
segments.summary: Josh promotes TryPod month, encouraging listeners to share podcasts. Hosts banter, including a British accent bit, and introduce the episode's foreign accent topic.

segments.title: Code switching and accent identity
segments.summary: Hosts describe code switching, adopting another person's accent, and why group members tease it. Chuck recalls his mom imitating an Irish woman's accent. They mention a Judge John Hodgman case about a mother using accents.

segments.title: Foreign accent syndrome defined and Lisa Arlami case
segments.summary: FAS is contrasted with voluntary accent imitation as involuntary and rare, with about 150 documented cases. Lisa Arlami of Texas developed a British-sounding accent after jaw surgery.

segments.title: Astrid of Norway and naming the syndrome
segments.summary: Astrid, a Norwegian woman injured by German bomb shrapnel in WWII, woke with a German-sounding accent and was shunned. Neurologist Herman Monrad-Krohn coined an early term, and Harry Whittaker later coined foreign accent syndrome and set four diagnostic criteria.

segments.title: Neurogenic, psychogenic and mixed types
segments.summary: FAS is classified as neurogenic (from brain trauma, stroke, MS), psychogenic (tied to psychological conditions, clearing with them), or mixed. Neurogenic cases have no cure and are treated with speech therapy. A US case of a woman with schizophrenia who spoke with a British accent is discussed.

segments.title: Sarah Colwill and how brain damage changes prosody
segments.summary: Sarah Colwill, an English woman whose migraines led to a Chinese-sounding accent, is described, along with her disabilities and identity struggles. The hosts discuss the difficulty of diagnosis and how damage to brain regions controlling prosody changes speech, including vowel and consonant substitutions.

segments.title: Is the accent only in the listener's ear?
segments.summary: Hosts debate whether FAS is only perceived by listeners, citing studies where listeners guessed different origins. They discuss that patients hear their speech as off, and that the predictable errors make it sound like an accent. They also cover a Dutch teacher who spoke Dutch with French features and speculate that FAS may split into separate syndromes.

segments.title: Closing discussion and search tip
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the topic, noting neural linguistics interest and suggesting listeners search How Stuff Works for foreign accent syndrome.

segments.title: Listener mail and thank-yous
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank listeners for gifts including calendars, coffee, chocolates, mayonnaise, a monocle, cutting board, and many handwritten letters and cards.
